31105-the-elements-of-agriculture-a-book:
G. E. Waring Jr.'s Elements of Agriculture, published by D. Appleton, is a textbook written for young farmers and schools in the 1850s, with questions for students printed at the foot of most pages. Chapters treat the formation and character of the soil, the character and varieties of manure, the mechanical character of the soil, and the nature of analysis.

An advertisement in the volume promises a larger sequel, The Earthworker, with fuller directions for manures and drainage. Practical rather than theoretical, the book teaches a farmer to test his ground, feed it wisely, and understand what his crops take from it. It remains a clear window on American farm science before the Civil War.
doe-osti-3001274-laser-confocal-microsco:
Jonathan Gigax and Gabriel Longoria of Los Alamos pin down how much to trust a microscope in LA-UR-25-27800, issued 8 November 2025. The instrument is a Keyence VK-3050 laser confocal microscope, used to measure pit depths in corroded container coupons, the small metal samples that stand sentry for stored materials. A 20x objective does the work, stitching image arrays across 25-millimetre coupons in runs that can stretch to 48 hours per coupon.

Uncertainty hides in stage travel, scan duration and repeatability. Repeated scans of calibration samples, ten at a time at fixed locations with minimised travel, separated the error sources. Z-axis motion over long height ranges proved a real contributor, and equipment on-time another. The bottom line is practical: a combined depth uncertainty of plus or minus 0.25 micrometres captures the observed error across the study. Corrosion scientists can now quote pit depths with an honest error bar attached.
doe-osti-3002985-molecular-dynamics-simu:
Ian Winter, Eric Rothchild, and Michael Chandross simulate brazing at atomic scale in Sandia report SAND2025-14027, printed November 2025. The question is how well liquid silver, standing in for a silver braze alloy, wets zirconia ceramics whose oxygen content varies. Wetting decides whether a braze joint spreads and holds or beads up and fails.

Molecular dynamics runs computed the work of adhesion between the liquid metal and four solids: zirconium metal, two suboxides, and full zirconia. The phantom wall method estimated adhesion, and Young's equation converted it to a wetting angle. The silver surface tension came out at 0.67 joules per square meter. Results show a wetting transition as oxygen content falls: leaner oxides bond differently. Braze designers use such maps when joining ceramics to metals.
doe-osti-3376047-thermal-performance-of-: Neutron sensors got thermal-performed, and this DOE text covers qualification devices. The pages detail the performance findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The device was qualification. The data were nuclear. The sensor were neutron. The qualification were device.
govdocs-archive_org-the-communist-party-: An FBI report in file HQ-116395, released under the Freedom of Information Act, examines the Communist Party USA and what the era called the Negro question. It records the party's stated position on Black Americans, as the bureau tracked it. The FBI watched the party for decades, and race was one of its constant concerns. The report shows both the party's line and the bureau's habits of watching it.
nasa-tm-19680018186-a-review-of-faciliti:
Seth B. Anderson and Laurel G. Schroers of Ames Research Center review low-speed flight test facilities and techniques in this paper. New classes of aircraft demand new and improved ways to test at low speed. Building novel aircraft is costly, so test methods must be trustworthy before full flight.

The authors survey the facilities available for low-speed work and the techniques used in them. They consider what new aircraft types require from those facilities. Gaps between current practice and future needs guide their review. The paper helps planners decide where to invest in test capability. It also helps engineers choose the right facility for a given low-speed program.
nasa-tm-19720019866-research-achievement:
Research Achievements Review, Volume 4, was issued May 30, 1972, as NASA TM X-64666. It covers quality and reliability assurance research at the Marshall Space Flight Center. The center's Science and Engineering Directorate published the review. Its theme, per the catalog record, is newer approaches to reliability engineering and quality control for aerospace work.

The contents open with two imaging studies. One develops solid-state radiographic X-ray image amplifiers, panels that make X-ray pictures without film. Tables and figures compare those panels with fluoroscopes and show images of a luggage interior and the inner fixture of a graphite-epoxy strut. A second study presents a neutron-radiation imaging system, with its own comparison tables. Together they show Marshall's quality researchers building better ways to inspect hardware without taking it apart.
podcast-dannyjones-xDTCN86kcQU:
Dead Sea Scrolls scholar Kipp Davis joins Danny Jones to say he lost his faith after he decoded the oldest Bible texts. Davis is a scholar of the scrolls and the Hebrew Bible. His tale is one of a faith undone by study.

Davis tells how years with the scrolls showed him cracks in the tales he was raised on. He walks through what the old texts truly say and where they clash with the church's tale. Jones asks what he holds to now. Listeners get a rare tale of a scholar whose work cost him his creed. The library holds the talk as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-0CrBPwS8OqU:
Welterweight fighter Daniel Rodriguez headlines Rogan's MMA Show number 180. Rodriguez built his record the hard way, through grit and volume. His style favors pressure and tough exchanges.

Rogan reviews his fights and what makes his game work. They talk about camps, cuts, and the grind below the spotlight. Rodriguez shares his path from hard years to the big stage. The episode suits fans who love working fighters more than stars: men who earn each shot and talk about the cost without complaint. Respect runs under every exchange in the room.
